chapter.name: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round

questions.q: In this chapter, a circle is defined as the set of all points on a plane that are
questions.a: equidistant from a given point on that plane, the centre.
o: equidistant from a given point on that plane
equidistant from a given line on that plane
enclosed by a closed curve that has no corners
inside a fixed distance from a given point on that plane

questions.q: A glass bangle has an inner radius of 3.2 cm. A thin stick is placed straight across the inside of the bangle with both its ends touching the inner edge. What is the greatest possible length of the stick?
questions.a: 6.4 cm, the diameter, because the diameter is the longest chord: 2 x 3.2 = 6.4 cm.

questions.q: Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II. Column I: 1. Centre; 2. Radius; 3. Chord; 4. Diameter. Column II: A. A line segment joining two points of the circle; B. The fixed point from which all points of the circle are equally far; C. A chord that passes through the centre; D. The distance from the centre to any point of the circle.
questions.a: 1-B, 2-D, 3-A, 4-C: the centre is the fixed point, the radius is the distance from it to the circle, a chord joins two points of the circle, and a diameter is a chord through the centre.

questions.q: True or False: A circle of radius 4 cm has exactly one chord that is 8 cm long. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. A chord 8 cm long is 2 x 4 cm, the diameter, and every line through the centre gives a diameter, so the circle has infinitely many chords 8 cm long.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: an 8 cm chord is a diameter, and there are infinitely many diameters, one through the centre in every direction

questions.q: A circular iron well cover has radius 45 cm. (a) What is the length of its diameter? (b) Can a straight rod 1 m long lie across the cover with both ends on its edge? (c) How many lines of reflection symmetry does the circular cover have?
questions.a: (a) 2 x 45 = 90 cm. (b) No. The longest chord of a circle is its diameter, 90 cm, and 1 m = 100 cm is longer than that. (c) Infinitely many: every diameter is a line of reflection symmetry.
s: (a) Diameter = 90 cm
(b) No, since 100 cm is more than the longest chord, the 90 cm diameter
(c) Infinitely many, one along every diameter

questions.q: Assertion (A): The longest chord of a circle of radius 6 cm is 12 cm long. Reason (R): A circle looks exactly the same after it is rotated about its centre through any angle.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A is true because the longest chord is the diameter (p. 105), 2 x 6 = 12 cm; R states the rotational symmetry of a circle (p. 94), which does not explain the length of the longest chord.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A circle has centre O and radius 9 cm. Consider the following statements. I. A chord of this circle that is 18 cm long must pass through O. II. Like a square, this circle has exactly four lines of reflection symmetry. III. The locus of points on the plane that are 9 cm from O is this circle. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. A chord of length 18 cm equals the diameter, so it passes through O; the circle is the locus of points 9 cm from O. Statement II is wrong: every diameter is a line of symmetry, so there are infinitely many.

questions.q: Two points A and B are marked on a sheet of paper. (a) A point P lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB and is 9 cm from A. How far is P from B? (b) A point Q is 9 cm from A and 11 cm from B. Can Q lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 9 cm, because every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equidistant from A and B. (b) No. Every point of the perpendicular bisector is equally far from A and B, but QA = 9 cm and QB = 11 cm are not equal.
s: (a) PB = 9 cm because points on the perpendicular bisector are equidistant from A and B
(b) No, because QA and QB are unequal

questions.q: Kavya says: 'When I fold a paper circle so that the two parts of its boundary overlap exactly, the crease can be any chord of the circle; it need not pass through the centre.' Check her claim and say what the crease must be.
questions.a: Her claim is wrong. A chord that does not pass through the centre cuts the circle into a larger part (containing the centre) and a smaller part, so the two parts cannot fit on each other. For the boundaries to overlap exactly the crease must be a line of reflection symmetry, which passes through the centre: it is a diameter.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Reason: a chord not through the centre divides the circle into unequal parts that cannot overlap
The crease is a line of reflection symmetry through the centre, that is, a diameter

questions.q: Jamuna has a circular piece of paper and wants to find its centre. Amina tells her: 'Fold it so the edges overlap, open it, fold it again along a different line so the edges overlap, and open it. The point where the two creases cross is the centre.' (a) What is each crease, in terms of the circle? (b) Why must each crease pass through the centre? (c) Why do the two creases meet at exactly one point, and why is that point the centre? (d) One crease measures 21 cm from edge to edge. What is the radius of the paper circle? (e) If Jamuna makes a third such fold, where will the new crease cross the first two? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Each crease is a line of reflection symmetry of the circle, that is, a diameter. (b) Every line of reflection symmetry of a circle is a diameter, and a diameter is a chord through the centre. (c) Two different straight lines meet in at most one point; both creases contain the centre, so they meet only at the centre. (d) The crease is a diameter of 21 cm, so the radius is 10.5 cm. (e) At the same point, the centre, because the third crease is also a diameter and every diameter passes through the centre.
s: (a) Each crease is a line of reflection symmetry, a diameter
(b) A diameter passes through the centre
(c) Two different lines meet in one point; both contain the centre, so that point is the centre
(d) Radius = 21 / 2 = 10.5 cm
(e) The third crease also passes through the centre, the same point

questions.q: The centre of the circle that passes through all three vertices of a triangle is called the
questions.a: circumcentre of the triangle.

questions.q: A triangle has angles 40, 60 and 80 degrees. Where does the centre of the circle through its three vertices lie?
questions.a: Inside the triangle, because every angle is less than 90 degrees, so the triangle is acute-angled.
o: At the midpoint of the longest side
At the vertex with the largest angle

questions.q: (a) What is meant by the circumcircle of a triangle? (b) Which lines meet at the centre of the circumcircle?
questions.a: (a) The circumcircle is the circle that passes through all three vertices of the triangle. (b) The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of the triangle meet at its centre, the circumcentre.
s: (a) The circle passing through all three vertices
(b) The perpendicular bisectors of the sides

questions.q: True or False: Through any three points marked on a page, one circle can always be drawn. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. If the three points are collinear (on one straight line), no circle passes through all three. Only three non-collinear points always have exactly one circle through them.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: no circle passes through three collinear points; the result holds only for non-collinear points

questions.q: Triangle PQR has a right angle at Q, with PQ = 12 cm and QR = 16 cm. (a) Find the length of PR. (b) Where is the circumcentre of the triangle? (c) Find the circumradius.
questions.a: (a) PR^2 = 12^2 + 16^2 = 144 + 256 = 400, so PR = 20 cm. (b) For a right-angled triangle the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse PR. (c) The circumradius is half of PR, 10 cm.
s: (a) PR = 20 cm
(b) The circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse PR
(c) Circumradius = 10 cm

questions.q: Two points A and B are 56 cm apart. A circle of radius 53 cm is to pass through both A and B. Where can its centre be?
questions.a: At two positions, each 45 cm from the midpoint of AB, one on each side of AB. The centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and with half of AB = 28 cm and radius 53 cm, its distance from the midpoint is the square root of (2809 - 784) = 45 cm, on either side.
o: At two points, each 45 cm from the midpoint of AB, on opposite sides of AB
At one point only, 45 cm from the midpoint of AB
At two points, each 25 cm from the midpoint of AB, on opposite sides of AB
At every point of the perpendicular bisector of AB

questions.q: A and B are two points on a plane. Consider the following statements. I. The centres of all circles through A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB. II. Among all circles through A and B, there is one with the largest radius. III. Two different circles through A and B can have equal radii. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Every point equidistant from A and B is on the perpendicular bisector. Statement II is wrong: the radius keeps growing as the centre moves farther along the bisector, so there is no largest circle. Statement III is right: two centres at the same distance from AB on opposite sides give two different circles with equal radii.

questions.q: O is the circumcentre of triangle ABC and OA = 7 cm. (a) Find OB and OC, with a reason. (b) If angle OBC = 25 degrees, find angle OCB and angle BOC.
questions.a: (a) OB = OC = 7 cm, because the circumcentre is equally far from all three vertices. (b) Triangle OBC is isosceles with OB = OC, so angle OCB = 25 degrees, and angle BOC = 180 - 25 - 25 = 130 degrees.
s: (a) OB = OC = 7 cm, as the circumcentre is equidistant from the vertices
(b) Angle OCB = 25 degrees and angle BOC = 130 degrees

questions.q: Ritu marks three points A, B and C with AB = 8 cm, BC = 15 cm and AC = 17 cm. She says the centre of the circle through A, B and C lies inside triangle ABC. Is she right? Explain, and give the radius of the circle.
questions.a: She is not right. 8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2, so triangle ABC is right-angled at B. The circumcentre of a right-angled triangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse AC, which lies on a side, not inside. The radius is 17 / 2 = 8.5 cm.
s: Shows 8^2 + 15^2 = 17^2, so the triangle is right-angled at B
The circumcentre is the midpoint of AC, on the side, so Ritu is wrong
Radius = 8.5 cm

questions.q: Three villages P, Q and R are at P (1, 2), Q (9, 2) and R (2, 9) on a map grid marked in kilometres. A health centre is to be built at the point O that is equally far from all three villages. (a) O lies on the perpendicular bisector of PQ. Find the midpoint of PQ and say which vertical grid line this bisector is. (b) Take O on that line and use OP = OR to find the position of O. (c) Find how far the health centre is from each village. (d) Decide whether O lies inside triangle PQR, outside it, or on one of its sides. Justify your decision using the squares of the side lengths.
questions.a: (a) The midpoint of PQ is (5, 2). PQ is horizontal, so its perpendicular bisector is the vertical line x = 5. (b) Take O = (5, y). OP^2 = 16 + (y - 2)^2 and OR^2 = 9 + (y - 9)^2. Setting them equal: 16 + y^2 - 4y + 4 = 9 + y^2 - 18y + 81, so 14y = 70 and y = 5. O = (5, 5). (c) OP^2 = 16 + 9 = 25, OQ^2 = 16 + 9 = 25 and OR^2 = 9 + 16 = 25, so the centre is 5 km from each village. (d) PQ^2 = 64, PR^2 = 50 and QR^2 = 98. The largest, 98, is less than 64 + 50 = 114, so the angle at P is acute and so are the other two: the triangle is acute-angled, and the circumcentre O lies inside it.
s: (a) Midpoint (5, 2); the perpendicular bisector is the line x = 5
(b) OP = OR gives y = 5, so O = (5, 5)
(c) 5 km from each village
(d) 98 < 64 + 50, so the triangle is acute-angled and O lies inside it

questions.q: The chapter explains why equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre by showing two triangles are congruent. Which congruence rule does it use?
questions.a: SSS, because the two radii and the chord of one triangle equal the two radii and the chord of the other.

questions.q: In a circle with centre O, chords PQ and RS are equal in length and angle POQ = 72 degrees. What is angle ROS?
questions.a: 72 degrees, because equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre.

questions.q: O is the centre of a circle and OM is the perpendicular from O to the chord AB, meeting it at M. If AB = 18 cm, what is the length of AM?
questions.a: 9 cm, because the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.

questions.q: AB is a chord of a circle with centre O. (a) Why is triangle OAB isosceles? (b) If angle OAB = 40 degrees, find angle AOB.
questions.a: (a) OA and OB are both radii, so OA = OB and the triangle is isosceles. (b) Angle OBA = angle OAB = 40 degrees, so angle AOB = 180 - 40 - 40 = 100 degrees.
s: (a) OA = OB as both are radii
(b) Angle AOB = 100 degrees

questions.q: PQ is a chord of a circle with centre O, and M is the midpoint of PQ. (a) What angle does OM make with PQ? (b) If PQ = 14 cm, find PM. (c) Another chord RS of the same circle is also 14 cm long and angle POQ = 100 degrees. Find angle ROS.
questions.a: (a) 90 degrees: the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord. (b) PM = 14 / 2 = 7 cm. (c) 100 degrees, because equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre.
s: (a) OM is perpendicular to PQ, 90 degrees
(b) PM = 7 cm
(c) Angle ROS = 100 degrees

questions.q: Assertion (A): Two chords of a circle that each subtend 65 degrees at the centre are equal in length. Reason (R): Two chords of a circle that subtend equal angles at the centre are always parallel to each other.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. By Theorem 3 chords subtending equal angles at the centre are equal (SAS congruence). They need not be parallel: rotating one chord about the centre gives an equal chord in a different direction.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: A chord of a circle of radius 5 cm and a chord of a circle of radius 8 cm each subtend 90 degrees at their own centres, so the two chords are equal in length. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The result "equal angles at the centre give equal chords" holds only for chords of the same circle (or of circles with equal radii). Here each chord is the hypotenuse of a right isosceles triangle of two radii: the chords are 5 x the square root of 2, about 7.1 cm, and 8 x the square root of 2, about 11.3 cm.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the theorem needs the same circle; the chords are about 7.1 cm and 11.3 cm by Pythagoras

questions.q: In a circle with centre O, Neel draws chords AB and CD of equal length. He reports that angle AOB = 70 degrees and angle COD = 80 degrees. Show that his measurements cannot both be right.
questions.a: OA = OB = OC = OD, since all are radii, and AB = CD is given. So triangles OAB and OCD are congruent by SSS. Corresponding angles AOB and COD must then be equal, but 70 degrees is not equal to 80 degrees, so at least one measurement is wrong.
s: OA = OC and OB = OD as radii, and AB = CD
Triangles OAB and OCD are congruent by SSS
So angle AOB must equal angle COD; 70 and 80 degrees cannot both be right

questions.q: In a circle with centre O and radius 41 cm, chords AB and CD are each 80 cm long. M is the midpoint of AB. (a) Prove that OM is perpendicular to AB. (b) Find the length of OM. (c) Explain why angle AOB = angle COD. (d) N is the foot of the perpendicular from O to CD. Explain why N is the midpoint of CD, and find ON.
questions.a: (a) OA = OB (radii), AM = BM (M is the midpoint) and OM is common, so triangles OMA and OMB are congruent (SSS). Hence angle OMA = angle OMB, and since they add to 180 degrees, each is 90 degrees. (b) AM = 40 cm, so OM^2 = 41^2 - 40^2 = 1681 - 1600 = 81 and OM = 9 cm. (c) AB = CD, and equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre (triangles OAB and OCD are congruent by SSS). (d) The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it, so CN = 40 cm and ON = the square root of (1681 - 1600) = 9 cm.
s: (a) Congruent triangles OMA and OMB, so angle OMA = angle OMB = 90 degrees
(b) OM = 9 cm
(c) Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre (SSS)
(d) The perpendicular from the centre bisects CD; ON = 9 cm

questions.q: A craftsperson fixes straight brass strips across a circular plate with centre O and radius 20 cm, each strip having both ends on the rim. Strip AB is 32 cm long. She drills a hole at the midpoint M of the strip and runs a straight wire from O to M. (a) What angle does the wire OM make with the strip AB? (b) Find the lengths of AM and OM. (c) A second strip CD is drilled at its midpoint N, and ON also turns out to be 12 cm. How long is CD, and how do the angles AOB and COD compare? (d) She wants a third strip whose wire to its midpoint is only 6 cm long. Find the length of that strip and say whether it is longer or shorter than AB.
questions.a: (a) 90 degrees, since the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it. (b) AM = 16 cm and OM = the square root of (400 - 256) = 12 cm. (c) CD is also 12 cm from O, so its half is the square root of (400 - 144) = 16 cm and CD = 32 cm; equal chords subtend equal angles, so angle AOB = angle COD. (d) Half the strip is the square root of (400 - 36) = about 19.08 cm, so the strip is about 38.2 cm, longer than AB: a chord closer to the centre is longer.
s: (a) OM is perpendicular to AB, 90 degrees
(b) AM = 16 cm and OM = 12 cm
(c) CD = 32 cm and angle COD = angle AOB
(d) About 38.2 cm, longer than AB

questions.q: A chord of a circle of radius 10 cm is 6 cm from the centre. What is the length of the chord?
questions.a: 16 cm: half the chord is the square root of (100 - 36) = 8 cm, so the chord is 16 cm.

questions.q: Two chords of the same circle are 9 cm and 15 cm long. Which chord is closer to the centre?
questions.a: The 15 cm chord, because of two unequal chords the longer one is closer to the centre.
o: Both are at the same distance
It cannot be decided without the radius

questions.q: (a) Two chords of the same circle are each 5 cm from the centre. What can you say about their lengths? (b) Which chord of a circle is at distance zero from the centre?
questions.a: (a) They are equal in length, because chords equidistant from the centre are equal. (b) A diameter, since it passes through the centre.
s: (a) The chords are equal
(b) A diameter

questions.q: A circular dining-table top has radius 65 cm. Straight strips of tape are stuck across it, each with both ends on the edge. (a) Find the length of a strip 16 cm from the centre. (b) Find the length of a strip 33 cm from the centre. (c) Find the length of a strip 60 cm from the centre. (d) Which of these three strips is closest to the centre, and is it the longest? (e) How far from the centre is a strip 130 cm long?
questions.a: Using chord length = 2 x the square root of (r^2 - d^2): (a) 2 x 63 = 126 cm. (b) 2 x 56 = 112 cm. (c) 2 x 25 = 50 cm. (d) The strip 16 cm from the centre is closest, and it is the longest, as the longer chord is closer to the centre. (e) 130 cm = 2 x 65 cm is the diameter, so it is 0 cm from the centre.
s: (c) 50 cm
(d) The 16 cm strip is closest and longest
(e) 0 cm, it is a diameter

questions.q: A circle has radius 29 cm. (a) Find the distance from the centre of a chord 42 cm long. (b) Find the distance from the centre of a chord 40 cm long. (c) Which chord is closer to the centre?
questions.a: (a) Half the chord is 21 cm, so the distance is the square root of (841 - 441) = 20 cm. (b) Half the chord is 20 cm, so the distance is the square root of (841 - 400) = 21 cm. (c) The 42 cm chord, at 20 cm; the longer chord is closer to the centre.
s: (a) 20 cm
(b) 21 cm
(c) The 42 cm chord is closer

questions.q: Match each situation in Column I with its value in Column II. Column I: 1. Length of a chord 80 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 89 cm; 2. Distance from the centre of a chord 130 cm long in a circle of radius 97 cm; 3. Radius of a circle in which a chord 40 cm long is 99 cm from the centre; 4. Distance from the centre of a chord 194 cm long in a circle of radius 97 cm. Column II: A. 0 cm; B. 72 cm; C. 78 cm; D. 101 cm.
questions.a: 1-C, 2-B, 3-D, 4-A: 2 x the square root of (7921 - 6400) = 2 x 39 = 78; the square root of (9409 - 4225) = 72; the square root of (400 + 9801) = 101; a 194 cm chord is a diameter, at 0 cm.

questions.q: True or False: In a circle of radius 73 cm, a chord 48 cm from the centre is longer than a chord 55 cm from the centre by exactly 14 cm. Show the lengths.
questions.a: True. The chord 48 cm away is 2 x the square root of (5329 - 2304) = 2 x 55 = 110 cm and the chord 55 cm away is 2 x the square root of (5329 - 3025) = 2 x 48 = 96 cm, and 110 - 96 = 14 cm.
s: Verdict: True
Lengths 110 cm and 96 cm, difference 14 cm

questions.q: Sanjay says: 'If one chord of a circle is twice as long as another, it is half as far from the centre.' Test his claim in a circle of radius 85 cm using a chord 26 cm long and a chord 52 cm long, and give your verdict.
questions.a: The 26 cm chord has half-length 13 cm, so its distance from the centre is the square root of (7225 - 169) = 84 cm. The 52 cm chord has half-length 26 cm, so its distance is the square root of (7225 - 676) = the square root of 6549, about 80.9 cm. Half of 84 cm is 42 cm, not 80.9 cm, so the claim is false: the distance is the square root of (r^2 - (half-chord)^2), not a fixed fraction of the chord length.
s: 26 cm chord is 84 cm from the centre
52 cm chord is about 80.9 cm from the centre
80.9 is not 42, so the claim is false

questions.q: Consider all the chords of length 120 cm in a circle with centre O and radius 61 cm. (a) Show that the midpoint of each such chord is 11 cm from O. (b) What shape do the midpoints of all these chords form? (c) Can a chord 120 cm long have its midpoint 10 cm from O? Give a reason. (d) Describe the shape formed by the midpoints of all chords 22 cm long in the same circle. (e) Which set of midpoints is closer to O, and which result about chords does this match?
questions.a: (a) The line from O to the midpoint is perpendicular to the chord, so with half-chord 60 cm, the distance is the square root of (3721 - 3600) = 11 cm. (b) A circle with centre O and radius 11 cm. (c) No. A chord whose midpoint is 10 cm from O has length 2 x the square root of (3721 - 100) = 2 x the square root of 3621, about 120.3 cm, not 120 cm. (d) Half-chord 11 cm gives distance the square root of (3721 - 121) = 60 cm, so the midpoints form a circle with centre O and radius 60 cm. (e) The midpoints of the 120 cm chords are closer to O, matching the result that the longer chord is closer to the centre.
s: (a) Distance = 11 cm using the perpendicular from O and half-chord 60 cm
(b) A circle with centre O and radius 11 cm
(c) No, such a chord is about 120.3 cm long
(d) A circle with centre O and radius 60 cm
(e) The 120 cm chords' midpoints are closer; the longer chord is closer to the centre

questions.q: A gram panchayat plans two straight, parallel footbridges across a circular village pond of radius 37 m, each with both ends on the bank. Bridge P will be 12 m from the fountain at the centre of the pond, and bridge Q will be 35 m from it, on the opposite side of the fountain. A contractor charges Rs 4,500 per metre of bridge. (a) Find the length of bridge P. (b) Find the length of bridge Q. (c) How far apart are the two bridges? (d) The budget is Rs 4,50,000. Can both bridges be built, and how much money is left over or short?
questions.a: (a) 2 x the square root of (1369 - 144) = 2 x 35 = 70 m. (b) 2 x the square root of (1369 - 1225) = 2 x 12 = 24 m. (c) They are on opposite sides of the centre, so 12 + 35 = 47 m apart. (d) Total length 94 m costs 94 x 4,500 = Rs 4,23,000, which is within the budget, leaving Rs 27,000.
s: (a) Bridge P = 70 m
(b) Bridge Q = 24 m
(c) 47 m apart
(d) Cost Rs 4,23,000, so both can be built with Rs 27,000 left

questions.q: An arc of a circle subtends an angle of 124 degrees at the centre. What angle does it subtend at a point on the circle outside the arc?
questions.a: 62 degrees, because the angle at the centre is double the angle at a point on the circle outside the arc.

questions.q: AB is a diameter of a circular steel plate, and P is any point on the rim other than A and B. What is angle APB?
questions.a: 90 degrees, because the angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circle is 90 degrees.
o: It depends on where P is

questions.q: Assertion (A): P and Q are two points on a circle, both outside the arc AB, so angle APB = angle AQB. Reason (R): Each of these angles is half the angle subtended by the arc AB at the centre.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: by Theorem 9 each angle is half the angle at the centre, so the two angles are equal.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A and B are points on a circle with centre O. The minor arc AXB subtends 80 degrees at O. (a) What angle does the arc AXB subtend at a point C on the circle outside the arc? (b) What angle does the major arc AYB subtend at O?
questions.a: (a) Half of 80 degrees, that is 40 degrees. (b) Sweeping from OA to OB the other way round gives 360 - 80 = 280 degrees.
s: (a) 40 degrees
(b) 280 degrees

questions.q: An open-air theatre has a circular boundary wall with centre O. The two ends A and B of a straight screen are fixed on the wall, and AB is not a diameter. Seats S1, S2 and S3 are placed on the wall, all on the major arc, away from the screen. From seat S1 the ends of the screen are seen at an angle AS1B of 38 degrees. (a) What is angle AS2B at seat S2? (b) Find angle AOB at the centre. (c) Find angle OAB in triangle AOB. (d) If the screen were replaced by a wider one whose ends were the two ends of a diameter, at what angle would each seat see its ends?
questions.a: (a) 38 degrees, as angles subtended by the same arc at points of the circle outside it are equal. (b) Angle AOB = 2 x 38 = 76 degrees. (c) OA = OB, so angle OAB = (180 - 76) / 2 = 52 degrees. (d) 90 degrees, the angle in a semicircle.
s: (a) Angle AS2B = 38 degrees
(b) Angle AOB = 76 degrees
(c) Angle OAB = 52 degrees
(d) 90 degrees

questions.q: Consider the following statements about a circle with centre O and a chord AB. I. The angle the minor arc AB subtends at O is twice the angle it subtends at any point of the circle outside that arc. II. A point outside the circle, on the same side of AB as a point P on the circle, sees AB at a smaller angle than angle APB. III. A diameter subtends 90 degrees at every point of the circle other than its ends. Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III. Statement I is Theorem 9; II is true because a point outside the circle on the same side of AB as P always sees AB at a smaller angle than a point on the circle; III is the angle-in-a-semicircle result.

questions.q: AB is a diameter of a circle and P is a point on the circle. Angle PAB = (3x) degrees and angle PBA = (2x) degrees. (a) Find angle APB, giving the reason. (b) Find x, and the angles PAB and PBA.
questions.a: (a) Angle APB = 90 degrees, because a diameter subtends 90 degrees at any point on the circle. (b) 3x + 2x = 180 - 90 = 90, so x = 18; angle PAB = 54 degrees and angle PBA = 36 degrees.
s: (a) 90 degrees, the angle in a semicircle
(b) x = 18, angles 54 and 36 degrees

questions.q: In a circle with centre O and radius 9 cm, the chord AB subtends an angle of 45 degrees at a point P on the major arc. Find angle AOB and the length of AB, giving reasons.
questions.a: Angle AOB = 2 x 45 = 90 degrees, since the angle at the centre is double the angle at a point on the circle outside the arc. OA = OB = 9 cm, so triangle AOB is right-angled at O and, by Pythagoras, AB^2 = 81 + 81 = 162, so AB = 9 x the square root of 2, about 12.7 cm.
s: Angle AOB = 90 degrees by Theorem 9
Triangle AOB is right-angled at O with OA = OB = 9 cm
AB = 9 x the square root of 2, about 12.7 cm

questions.q: A circular lawn has centre O and radius 20 m. Two lamps stand at points A and B on the boundary, 20 m apart. (a) Show that angle AOB = 60 degrees. (b) Find the angle at which a bench P on the major arc sees the two lamps. (c) Find the angle at which a bench Q on the minor arc sees the two lamps. (d) A guard stands at a point R inside the lawn, on the same side of AB as P. Explain why angle ARB is greater than angle APB. (e) If the lamps were moved to the two ends of a diameter, at what angle would P see them?
questions.a: (a) OA = OB = AB = 20 m, so triangle OAB is equilateral and angle AOB = 60 degrees. (b) Angle APB = 60 / 2 = 30 degrees. (c) Q sees the major arc, which subtends the reflex angle 360 - 60 = 300 degrees at O, so angle AQB = 150 degrees. (d) Extend AR to meet the circle at E on the major arc. Angle AEB = 30 degrees (same arc as P), and angle ARB is an exterior angle of triangle RBE, so it is greater than angle AEB = 30 degrees. (e) 90 degrees, the angle in a semicircle.
s: (a) Equilateral triangle OAB, so angle AOB = 60 degrees
(b) 30 degrees
(c) 150 degrees, half the reflex angle 300 degrees
(d) Extends AR to E on the circle; exterior angle ARB is greater than angle AEB = 30 degrees
(e) 90 degrees

questions.q: A, B, C and D are points on a circle. The chords AC and BD cross at a point P inside the circle. Angle BAC = 40 degrees and angle APB = 110 degrees. (a) Find angle ABD from triangle ABP. (b) Find angle BDC, giving the reason. (c) Find angle ACD, giving the reason. (d) Find angle CPD and show that triangles APB and DPC have the same three angles.
questions.a: (a) In triangle ABP, angle ABD = 180 - 40 - 110 = 30 degrees. (b) Angle BDC = angle BAC = 40 degrees, since both are subtended by the same arc BC at points of the circle on the same side (angles in the same segment are equal). (c) Angle ACD = angle ABD = 30 degrees, since both are subtended by arc AD at points on the same side. (d) Angle CPD = angle APB = 110 degrees (vertically opposite), and 40 + 30 + 110 = 180 checks triangle DPC; both triangles have angles 40, 30 and 110 degrees.
s: (a) Angle ABD = 30 degrees from the angle sum of triangle ABP
(b) Angle BDC = 40 degrees, same arc BC
(c) Angle ACD = 30 degrees, same arc AD
(d) Angle CPD = 110 degrees; both triangles have angles 40, 30, 110 degrees

questions.q: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle B = 68 degrees. What is angle D?
questions.a: 112 degrees, because opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees.

questions.q: Points that lie on the same circle are called
questions.a: concyclic points.

questions.q: PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral, with its vertices taken in order round the circle. Which pair of its angles must add up to 180 degrees?
questions.a: Angle P and angle R, because they are opposite angles, and the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees.

questions.q: In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, the angles A, B and C are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. (a) Which two of these three angles add up to 180 degrees, and why? (b) Taking angle A = 2k, angle B = 3k and angle C = 4k, find k. (c) Find angles A, B and C. (d) Find angle D.
questions.a: (a) Angle A and angle C, because they are opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, and opposite angles add up to 180 degrees. (b) 2k + 4k = 180, so 6k = 180 and k = 30. (c) Angle A = 60 degrees, angle B = 90 degrees and angle C = 120 degrees. (d) Angle D = 180 - angle B = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees.
s: (a) A and C, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral
(c) A = 60, B = 90, C = 120 degrees
(d) D = 90 degrees

questions.q: (a) What is a cyclic quadrilateral? (b) A rhombus has angles 60, 120, 60 and 120 degrees in order. Can it be a cyclic quadrilateral? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) A quadrilateral whose four vertices all lie on one circle. (b) No. Its opposite angles are 60 and 60 degrees, which add to 120 degrees, not 180 degrees, so it cannot be cyclic.
s: (a) A quadrilateral whose vertices lie on one circle
(b) No, opposite angles add to 120 degrees, not 180 degrees

questions.q: Assertion (A): A cyclic quadrilateral whose four angles are all equal must be a square. Reason (R): The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. R is Theorem 11. If all four angles are equal, each is 90 degrees, so the quadrilateral is a rectangle; a rectangle with unequal sides is cyclic but is not a square.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Points C and D lie on the same side of a segment AB, and angle ACB = angle ADB = 47 degrees. A point E on the other side of AB has angle AEB = 133 degrees. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: All five points A, B, C, D and E lie on one circle: C and D are concyclic with A and B by Theorem 10, and in quadrilateral ACBE the opposite angles at C and E add to 47 + 133 = 180 degrees, so E is on the same circle.
o: All five points A, B, C, D and E lie on one circle
A, B, C and D lie on one circle, but E does not
Only A, B and C are certain to lie on one circle
E is the centre of the circle through A, B and C

questions.q: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral. Side AB is extended beyond B to a point E, and the exterior angle CBE = 74 degrees. (a) Find angle ABC. (b) Find angle ADC, giving the reason.
questions.a: (a) Angle ABC = 180 - 74 = 106 degrees, angles on a line. (b) Angle ADC = 180 - 106 = 74 degrees, because opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180 degrees.
s: (a) Angle ABC = 106 degrees
(b) Angle ADC = 74 degrees, opposite angles add to 180 degrees

questions.q: A circular park has four gates W, X, Y and Z on its fence, in that order around the circle. The straight path WX passes through the fountain at the centre of the park, so WX is a diameter. A gardener measures angle ZXW = 18 degrees. (a) Find angle WZX, giving the reason. (b) Find angle ZWX. (c) Find angle XYZ. (d) The gardener says gate Y sees the path WZ at the same angle as gate X does. Is she right? Find both angles.
questions.a: (a) Angle WZX = 90 degrees, since the diameter WX subtends 90 degrees at Z on the circle. (b) Angle ZWX = 180 - 90 - 18 = 72 degrees. (c) WXYZ is a cyclic quadrilateral, so angle XYZ = 180 - angle XWZ = 180 - 72 = 108 degrees. (d) Yes. X and Y both lie on the circle outside the arc WZ that does not contain them, so angle WYZ = angle WXZ = 18 degrees.
s: (a) Angle WZX = 90 degrees, angle in a semicircle
(b) Angle ZWX = 72 degrees
(c) Angle XYZ = 108 degrees, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral
(d) Yes, both angles are 18 degrees (angles subtended by the same arc)

questions.q: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral whose circle has centre O, and O lies inside ABCD. B and D are joined to O. The angle at O swept from OB to OD on the side where C lies is 130 degrees. (a) Find angle BAD, giving the reason. (b) What angle does the arc BAD subtend at O? (c) Find angle BCD. (d) If the angle at O on the side of C is x degrees instead, show that angle BAD + angle BCD is always 180 degrees. (e) Find angle OBD.
questions.a: (a) A lies outside the arc BCD, which subtends 130 degrees at O, so angle BAD = 130 / 2 = 65 degrees. (b) The arc BAD subtends the rest of the full turn, 360 - 130 = 230 degrees. (c) C lies outside the arc BAD, so angle BCD = 230 / 2 = 115 degrees. (d) Angle BAD = x / 2 and angle BCD = (360 - x) / 2, so their sum is 360 / 2 = 180 degrees. (e) OB = OD (radii), so angle OBD = (180 - 130) / 2 = 25 degrees.
s: (a) Angle BAD = 65 degrees, half the angle of arc BCD at O
(b) 230 degrees
(c) Angle BCD = 115 degrees
(d) x / 2 + (360 - x) / 2 = 180 for every x
(e) Angle OBD = 25 degrees from isosceles triangle OBD
